overview.title: Building the MNIST network: layers and the compilation step
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.1 A first look at a neural network
overview.main_topic: Defining a two-layer Dense network for MNIST with `keras.Sequential`, the idea of a layer as a data filter, and the three ingredients chosen at compilation: loss function, optimizer and metrics.
overview.central_idea: A neural network is a chain of layers that progressively distill data into more useful representations; before it can learn, it must be compiled with a loss function (how to measure error), an optimizer (how to update the weights) and metrics (what to monitor).
overview.importance: This page introduces the two most fundamental Keras abstractions the whole book builds on: the layer (and the `Sequential` stack of layers) and the compile step. Every later model in the book, from convnets to Transformers, is a variation on this exact pattern: define layers, compile with loss/optimizer/metrics, then fit.
learning_objectives: Read Listing 2.2 and explain what `keras.Sequential` and the two `layers.Dense` calls construct.
Describe a layer as a data filter that extracts representations, and a model as a chain of such filters (progressive data distillation).
Explain why the last layer has 10 units with a `softmax` activation and what its output represents.
Name the three things fixed at compilation (loss function, optimizer, metrics) and state the role of each.
prerequisites: The MNIST dataset and the train/test arrays loaded on p.42 (`train_images`, `train_labels`, `test_images`, `test_labels`).
The chapter-1 picture of a network as a sequence of layers parameterized by weights, with a loss function as feedback signal and an optimizer that adjusts the weights (p.32-33).
Basic Python: imports, keyword arguments, lists.

summary:
This page finishes stating the workflow of the first example (train on `train_images`/`train_labels`, then predict on `test_images` and compare against `test_labels`) and then builds the network in **Listing 2.2**: a `keras.Sequential` model holding two `layers.Dense` layers, the first with 512 units and a `relu` activation, the second with 10 units and a `softmax` activation.

The authors then introduce the central abstraction of the chapter: the **layer**. A layer is described as a *filter for data*: data goes in and comes out in a more useful form. Layers *extract representations* from their inputs, ideally representations that are more meaningful for the task. Deep learning mostly consists of chaining simple layers so that the chain performs *progressive data distillation*; the model is compared to a **sieve** made of a succession of increasingly refined filters.

Applied to Listing 2.2: the model is a sequence of two `Dense` (densely connected, a.k.a. fully connected) layers. The last one is a *10-way softmax classification layer*: it returns an array of 10 probability scores that sum to 1, each being the probability that the current image belongs to one of the 10 digit classes.

To make the model trainable, three more choices are made in the **compilation step**:

- a **loss function**, which lets the model measure its performance on the training data and so steer itself in the right direction;
- an **optimizer**, the mechanism by which the model updates itself from the training data it sees;
- **metrics** to monitor during training and testing; here only **accuracy**, the fraction of correctly classified images.

The authors postpone the exact meaning of loss and optimizer to the next two chapters (this one and chapter 3). **Listing 2.3** (the compilation step) starts at the bottom of the page with `model.compile(optimizer="adam", ...` and continues on p.44.

paragraphs.excerpt: labels. Finally, we'll ask the network to produce predictions for test_images, and
paragraphs.what_it_says: This is the end of the sentence begun on p.42 describing the workflow: after the network has learned to associate `train_images` with `train_labels`, we will ask it to produce predictions for `test_images` and check whether those predictions match `test_labels`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The workflow has two phases that use disjoint data. Learning only ever sees the training arrays; evaluation uses images the model has never seen, so the comparison with `test_labels` measures how well the learned mapping *generalizes*, not how well it memorized.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Keeping a held-out test set separate from the training set is the single most basic discipline of machine learning; the book returns to it in depth when it discusses generalization and validation (chapter 5).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Supervised learning on a labeled dataset: fit a function `f` on `(train_images, train_labels)`, then score `f(test_images)` against `test_labels`.

terminology.meaning: The model's output for an input it is given; for MNIST, a guess (as class probabilities) of which digit an image shows.

connections: p.44: Listing 2.6 actually runs the prediction on test digits.

paragraphs.what_it_says: A transitional line: the authors are about to show the model code and reassure the reader that full understanding is not expected yet.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Section 2.1 is a deliberately 'look first, understand later' tour. The concepts needed to really understand Listing 2.2 (tensors, tensor operations, gradient descent) come in sections 2.2-2.4, and the example is revisited line by line in section 2.5 (p.75).

paragraphs.excerpt: The core building block of neural networks is the layer. You can think
paragraphs.what_it_says: The layer is the core building block of a neural network. A layer is a filter for data: some data goes in, and it comes out in a more useful form. Layers extract *representations* from their input, hopefully representations more meaningful for the problem at hand. Most of deep learning consists of chaining simple layers that together implement *progressive data distillation*; a model is like a *sieve* made of a succession of increasingly refined filters.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each layer is a transformation of its input, and in a deep model the transformations are composed. No single layer solves the task; the task is solved by the composition, with each stage producing a representation that makes the next stage's job easier. For MNIST, the first `Dense` layer turns 784 raw pixel intensities into 512 learned features, and the second turns those 512 features into 10 class scores.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the conceptual definition of 'deep' in deep learning: depth is the number of successive representation-refining layers. Every architecture in the book (convnets, RNNs, Transformers) is a different choice of what kind of filter the layers are, but all of them are chains of layers.
paragraphs.technical_idea: A layer is a function `f_i` from tensors to tensors (usually with learnable weights); the model is the composition `f_L(...f_2(f_1(x)))`. 'Representation' means the intermediate tensor produced at each stage.

terminology.meaning: A data-processing module that takes a tensor in and produces a tensor out, usually parameterized by learnable weights.
A different way of encoding the same data; here, the output of a layer, intended to be more useful for the task than its input.
The authors' phrase for how a chain of layers successively purifies the information relevant to the task.

connections: p.116: chapter 3 defines a layer more precisely as a module with weights learned by stochastic gradient descent.
p.32: chapter 1 described the same idea as 'a deep sequence of simple data transformations (layers)' learned from examples.

paragraphs.excerpt: Here, our model consists of a sequence of two Dense layers, which are
paragraphs.what_it_says: The model is a sequence of two `Dense` layers, also called densely connected or fully connected layers. The second and last layer is a 10-way `softmax` classification layer: it returns an array of 10 probability scores summing to 1, each the probability that the current image belongs to one of the 10 digit classes. Making the model ready for training requires three more choices, made in the compilation step.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Densely connected' means every output unit of the layer is connected to every input value (through a weight matrix). The final layer's width equals the number of classes (10 digits), and `softmax` turns the 10 raw scores into a probability distribution, so the model's output can be read directly as 'how confident am I that this is a 0, a 1, ..., a 9'.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This 'last layer = number of classes, activation = softmax' pattern is the standard recipe for multiclass classification and is reused for the 46-class Reuters example on p.143. Understanding that the output is a probability distribution is what makes the prediction on p.44 (index of the largest score = predicted class) make sense.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Each `Dense` layer computes `output = activation(dot(input, W) + b)` with a weight matrix `W` and bias vector `b` (shown explicitly on p.76). With 512 then 10 units, the first layer has a `(784, 512)` kernel and the second a `(512, 10)` kernel once the input shape is known.

terminology.meaning: A layer in which every output unit depends on every input value through a learned weight matrix plus a bias.
An activation that maps a vector of real scores to a vector of positive numbers summing to 1, interpretable as class probabilities.
The Keras call `model.compile(...)` that fixes the optimizer, loss and metrics before training.

connections: p.76: section 2.5 writes out the tensor operations each Dense layer performs.
p.143: the Reuters example uses the same 'Dense(46, softmax)' pattern for 46 classes.

paragraphs.excerpt: A loss function—How the model will be able to measure its performance on
paragraphs.what_it_says: The first compile ingredient is the loss function: how the model measures its performance on the training data and therefore how it can steer itself in the right direction.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The loss is a single number computed from predictions and true labels; lower is better. Because training is defined as 'reduce this number', the loss is literally the definition of what the model is trying to achieve.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Chapter 1 (p.33) called the loss the feedback signal of deep learning. Choosing a loss appropriate to the task (e.g. cross-entropy for classification, mean squared error for regression) is one of the recurring decisions in the book.
paragraphs.technical_idea: For this example the loss will be `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` (see p.44), which measures the distance between the predicted softmax distribution and the true class.

terminology.meaning: A function of predictions and targets producing a scalar score of how wrong the model is; also called objective or cost function.

connections: p.33: the loss function as the 'distance score' between prediction and target.
p.143: categorical cross-entropy explained as a distance between two probability distributions.

paragraphs.excerpt: An optimizer—The mechanism through which the model will update itself based
paragraphs.what_it_says: The second ingredient is the optimizer: the mechanism through which the model updates itself based on the training data it sees, to improve its performance.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The optimizer takes the loss (and its gradient with respect to the weights) and decides how to change the weights. In Listing 2.3 it is `"adam"`, a variant of stochastic gradient descent.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Section 2.4 of this chapter (p.63 onward) is entirely about what the optimizer does: gradient-based optimization and backpropagation.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Optimizers implement update rules of the form `W <- W - learning_rate * gradient(loss, W)` (plain SGD), possibly with momentum or per-parameter adaptive step sizes (Adam).

terminology.meaning: The algorithm that uses the loss gradient to update the model's weights.

connections: p.63: section 2.4 'The engine of neural networks: Gradient-based optimization'.
p.67: stochastic gradient descent, the family Adam belongs to.

paragraphs.excerpt: Metrics to monitor during training and testing—Here, we'll only care about
paragraphs.what_it_says: The third ingredient is the metrics to monitor during training and testing. For this example only accuracy matters: the fraction of images correctly classified.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Metrics are for humans; they do not drive the weight updates. Accuracy is easier to interpret than cross-entropy loss ('98.9 % of the digits were right') but it is not differentiable, so it cannot serve as the training loss.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Keeping loss (optimized) and metric (reported) separate is a distinction the book relies on constantly when reading training output such as the 0.989 accuracy shown on p.44.

terminology.meaning: Number of correctly classified samples divided by the total number of samples.

connections: p.44: `fit()` prints both the loss and the accuracy for each epoch.

paragraphs.excerpt: The exact purpose of the loss function and the optimizer will be made
paragraphs.what_it_says: The exact purpose of the loss function and the optimizer will be made clear throughout the next two chapters. Listing 2.3 then begins the compilation step: `model.compile(optimizer="adam", ...`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The reader is asked to accept the compile arguments on faith for now; section 2.4 and chapter 3 (p.97-99 printed, 'The compile step' and 'Picking a loss function') will fill in the meaning.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It tells you where to look when the three compile arguments stop feeling like magic strings.

concepts.name: Layer
concepts.definition: The core building block of a neural network: a data-processing module that takes data in and returns it transformed into a (hopefully) more useful representation.
concepts.intuition: A filter or sieve stage: raw data goes in, something more refined for the task comes out. Stack several and the chain progressively distills the information that matters.
concepts.technical: A layer is a function from input tensors to output tensors, typically parameterized by weight tensors learned during training. A `Dense` layer computes `activation(dot(input, W) + b)`.
concepts.significance: Deep learning is literally the practice of chaining many such layers; the architecture of a model is the choice of which layers to chain and how.
concepts.example: `layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")` maps each 784-value image vector to a 512-value feature vector.
concepts.misconception: A layer is not a single neuron and not the whole network; it is one transformation stage made of many units operating in parallel.

concepts.name: Dense (fully connected) layer
concepts.definition: A layer in which every output unit is connected to every input value by a learned weight, plus a bias, followed by an activation function.
concepts.intuition: Each of the layer's units looks at the entire input and computes one weighted 'opinion' about it; 512 units give 512 opinions.
concepts.technical: `output = activation(dot(input, W) + b)`, with `W` of shape `(input_dim, units)` and `b` of shape `(units,)`. Parameter count: `input_dim * units + units`.
concepts.significance: The simplest and most general layer; the MNIST model is made only of Dense layers, and Dense layers end almost every classifier in the book.
concepts.example: With a 784-dimensional input, `Dense(512)` has 784*512 + 512 = 401,920 parameters; `Dense(10)` after it has 512*10 + 10 = 5,130.
concepts.misconception: 'Dense' refers to connectivity, not to the number of units; a Dense layer with 2 units is still dense.

concepts.name: Sequential model
concepts.definition: A Keras model that is a plain stack of layers, each feeding the next, mapping a single input to a single output.
concepts.intuition: A pipeline: the output of layer 1 is the input of layer 2, and so on.
concepts.technical: `keras.Sequential([layer1, layer2, ...])`. Input shapes are inferred the first time data flows through, so Listing 2.2 does not state the 784-dimensional input shape.
concepts.significance: It is the simplest way to build a model and is sufficient for sections 2 to 6 of the book; chapter 7 introduces the Functional API and model subclassing for non-linear topologies (p.120).
concepts.misconception: Not every network is sequential; models with multiple inputs, multiple outputs or skip connections cannot be expressed with `Sequential` (p.120).

concepts.name: Softmax classification layer
concepts.definition: A final layer with as many units as classes and a softmax activation, so its output is a probability distribution over the classes.
concepts.intuition: Turn 10 raw scores into 10 shares of a single unit of confidence that add up to 1.
concepts.technical: `softmax(z)_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j)`. Every output is in (0, 1) and the outputs sum to exactly 1; the largest score corresponds to the largest logit.
concepts.significance: Gives the model's output a direct probabilistic reading and pairs naturally with the cross-entropy loss chosen on p.44.
concepts.example: On p.44 the first test digit gets probability 0.99999106 at index 7, so the model predicts a 7.
concepts.misconception: Softmax probabilities are the model's confidence, not guaranteed calibrated true probabilities; a 0.99 can still be wrong.

concepts.name: Loss function
concepts.definition: How the model measures its performance on the training data, and therefore how it can steer itself in the right direction.
concepts.intuition: A score of 'how wrong was I?' that training tries to drive down.
concepts.technical: A differentiable scalar function of predictions and targets; its gradient with respect to the weights is what the optimizer uses.
concepts.significance: It defines the objective of learning; chapter 1 called it the feedback signal (p.33).
concepts.example: For MNIST, `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` (p.44) between the softmax output and the integer label.
concepts.misconception: The loss is not the same as the metric: accuracy is reported but the loss is what is minimized.

concepts.name: Optimizer
concepts.definition: The mechanism through which the model updates itself based on the training data it sees, to improve its performance.
concepts.intuition: The part that turns 'I was wrong by this much' into 'nudge these weights this way'.
concepts.technical: An update rule applied to the weights using the loss gradient, e.g. SGD, RMSprop or Adam (used here as `optimizer="adam"`).
concepts.significance: Section 2.4 (p.63-74) is devoted to how optimizers work: derivatives, gradients, SGD and backpropagation.
concepts.misconception: The optimizer does not decide *what* to optimize; the loss does. The optimizer only decides *how* to move.

concepts.name: Metrics
concepts.definition: Quantities monitored during training and testing to judge the model; here, accuracy, the fraction of correctly classified images.
concepts.intuition: The scoreboard you watch, as opposed to the loss the model is pushed by.
concepts.technical: Metrics need not be differentiable because they are not used for gradient computation; accuracy = correct / total.
concepts.significance: Metrics are what you actually care about and report; the loss is often only a differentiable proxy for them.
concepts.example: `metrics=["accuracy"]` (continuation of Listing 2.3 on p.44) leads to the 0.989 training accuracy printed by `fit()`.
concepts.misconception: Monitoring a metric does not make the model optimize it.

math.title: What a Dense layer computes (stated later in the chapter)
math.source_text: output = relu(dot(input, W) + b) (made explicit on p.76; on this page only `layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")` appears)

variables.meaning: Input vector to the layer (for MNIST, 784 pixel values after flattening on p.44).
Weight matrix of shape (input size, units): (784, 512) for the first layer, (512, 10) for the second.
Bias vector with one entry per unit.
`relu` for the first layer, `softmax` for the second.

math.operations: A matrix product (every input weighted into every unit), a vector addition, then an element-wise (relu) or vector-wise (softmax) nonlinearity.
math.purpose: This is the tensor-level meaning of 'densely connected': every unit mixes all inputs through its own column of `W`.
math.interpretation: The dot product produces a new representation of the input; the activation decides which of those features are kept (relu) or how they are turned into probabilities (softmax).
math.intuition: Each of the 512 units is a weighted template matched against the whole image; relu keeps only positive matches.

math.title: Softmax: 10 scores summing to 1
math.source_text: "a 10-way softmax classification layer, which means it will return an array of 10 probability scores (summing to 1)"

variables.meaning: The 10 raw scores (logits) produced by the last Dense layer before the activation.
The raw score for digit class i.
The probability assigned to class i.

math.operations: Exponentiate each score (making all positive), then divide by the sum so the results add to 1.
math.purpose: Convert unconstrained scores into a probability distribution over the 10 digit classes.
math.interpretation: The output index with the largest probability is the model's predicted digit (used on p.44 with `argmax`).
math.intuition: Exponentiation sharpens differences: a score 2 units above the others gets about e^2 ≈ 7.4 times more probability.
math.numerical_example: Note (not in the book): for logits `[2, 1, 0]`, exp gives `[7.39, 2.72, 1.00]`, sum 11.11, so softmax ≈ `[0.665, 0.245, 0.090]`, which sums to 1.

code.title: The network architecture
code.original_code:
import keras
from keras import layers
model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        layers.Dense(512, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
    ]
)
code.what_it_does: Imports Keras and its `layers` module, then builds a `Sequential` model made of two Dense layers: a 512-unit hidden layer with relu activation and a 10-unit output layer with softmax activation.

line_explanations.explanation: Import the top-level `keras` package and the `layers` namespace that contains all built-in layer classes such as `Dense`.
`keras.Sequential(...)` takes a Python list of layers and chains them in order: the output of each becomes the input of the next.

First layer: 512 units, each computing a weighted sum of all input values plus a bias, followed by `relu` (negative values set to 0). Its input size is not written; Keras infers it (784) the first time data flows in.
Second and last layer: 10 units, one per digit class, with `softmax` so the 10 outputs are probabilities summing to 1.
Close the list and the constructor; `model` now holds an untrained network.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: once fitted on p.44, a float32 batch of shape `(batch, 784)`. Output: a batch of shape `(batch, 10)` of class probabilities.
code.algorithm: Forward pass: `h = relu(x · W1 + b1)` with `W1` of shape (784, 512); `p = softmax(h · W2 + b2)` with `W2` of shape (512, 10).
code.theory_link: This is the 'chain of layers = progressive data distillation' idea of the same page made concrete: 784 pixels -> 512 features -> 10 probabilities. The weights `W1, b1, W2, b2` are the parameters that training will set (p.32-33).

parameters.role: Number of units (output dimensionality) of the hidden layer; also the width of its weight matrix.

parameters.name: activation="relu"
parameters.role: Nonlinearity applied element-wise to the hidden layer's output: max(x, 0).
Number of units in the output layer, equal to the number of digit classes.

parameters.name: activation="softmax"
parameters.role: Converts the 10 output scores into a probability distribution.

pitfalls: The model has no weights until it sees an input (or `build()` is called), so `model.summary()` right after this listing will not show parameter counts.
The number of units in the last layer must equal the number of classes; using 9 or 11 here would make the loss on p.44 fail or be meaningless.
Forgetting `activation="softmax"` on the last layer would still run but the outputs would not be probabilities.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: inspect the shapes Keras will create once the input size is known
import numpy as np
model.build(input_shape=(None, 784))
for layer in model.layers:
    print(layer.name, [w.shape for w in layer.weights])
# dense   [(784, 512), (512,)]
# dense_1 [(512, 10), (10,)]
print(model.count_params())  # 407050

code.title: The compilation step (beginning; continues on p.44)
code.what_it_does: Starts the `compile()` call that configures the learning process. On this page only the optimizer argument is visible, set to the string `"adam"`; the loss and metrics arguments follow on p.44.

line_explanations.explanation: `model.compile(` begins configuring the model for training; nothing is trained yet.
`optimizer="adam"` selects the Adam optimizer by its string name; Keras instantiates it with default settings (learning rate 0.001).

code.inputs_outputs: Takes configuration arguments; returns nothing. After the full call (p.44) the model knows which loss to minimize, which optimizer to use, and which metrics to report.
code.algorithm: No computation happens at compile time; it only records the optimizer, loss and metrics objects used later by `fit()`.
code.theory_link: Implements the 'three more things' of the page: optimizer (how the weights are updated), loss (what is measured) and metrics (what is monitored).

parameters.name: optimizer
parameters.role: The weight-update mechanism; `"adam"` is an adaptive variant of stochastic gradient descent (SGD is introduced on p.67).

pitfalls: The listing is incomplete on this page; running these two lines alone is a syntax error. See p.44 for the closing arguments.
Passing a string uses default hyperparameters; to change the learning rate you would pass `keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=...)` instead.

deeper.title: The sieve analogy, stage by stage
deeper.body:
The authors compare a model to a sieve made of increasingly refined filters. Here is how the two layers of Listing 2.2 fit that picture.

1. **Raw material**: 784 pixel brightnesses. Individually they say almost nothing about which digit is shown.
2. **First filter (`Dense(512, relu)`)**: each of the 512 units weighs all 784 pixels and lights up (relu > 0) when a particular pattern of strokes is present. After training, these units behave like detectors for arcs, vertical bars, loops in certain positions. The data has been distilled from 'pixels' into 'stroke evidence'.
3. **Second filter (`Dense(10, softmax)`)**: each of the 10 units weighs the 512 pieces of stroke evidence and produces a score for one digit; softmax normalizes the scores into probabilities. The data has been distilled from 'stroke evidence' into 'which digit'.

Each stage throws away what the next stage does not need (that is the sieve) while keeping what matters for the task. The word 'hopefully' in the text is honest: nothing guarantees the intermediate representation is meaningful; training merely pushes it in that direction because that is what lowers the loss.

deeper.title: Why three things, and what each one is in this example
deeper.body:
| Compile ingredient | Role on this page | Value in the MNIST example | Where the book explains it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loss function | Measures performance on the training data so the model can steer itself | `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` (p.44) | p.33 (feedback signal), p.143 (cross-entropy as distance between distributions) |
| Optimizer | Mechanism by which the model updates itself | `"adam"` (this page) | Section 2.4, p.63-74 |
| Metrics | Monitored during training and testing | `["accuracy"]` (p.44) | Printed by `fit()` on p.44 |

A useful way to keep them apart (not in the book): the loss is *what the optimizer sees*, the optimizer is *how the weights move*, and the metric is *what you see*. Only the first two affect learning.

deeper.title: Counting the parameters of the network
deeper.body:
Beyond the book: the page says the layers are densely connected; here is what that implies in numbers once the input is flattened to 784 values (p.44).

- First layer: weight matrix `(784, 512)` = 401,408 weights, plus 512 biases = **401,920** parameters.
- Second layer: weight matrix `(512, 10)` = 5,120 weights, plus 10 biases = **5,130** parameters.
- Total: **407,050** learnable numbers.

These 407,050 values are exactly 'the knowledge of the model' that section 2.5 (p.76) says persists in the weight tensors, and they are what the optimizer named in Listing 2.3 will adjust. The rule used is `parameters = inputs * units + units` for each Dense layer.

misconceptions.claim: The 512 in `Dense(512)` is the number of input pixels.
misconceptions.correction: 512 is the number of units (outputs) of the layer. The input size (784 pixels) is not written in Listing 2.2; Keras infers it from the data on p.44.

misconceptions.claim: The compile step trains the model.
misconceptions.correction: Compilation only configures the learning process (optimizer, loss, metrics). Training happens in `fit()` on p.44.

misconceptions.claim: Accuracy is what the optimizer minimizes.
misconceptions.correction: The optimizer minimizes the loss function. Accuracy is a metric that is only monitored; it is not differentiable and is not used for weight updates.

misconceptions.claim: Each layer solves part of the task on its own, so a single big layer would work as well.

takeaways: A layer is a data filter that extracts a more useful representation; a deep model is a chain of such filters performing progressive data distillation.

questions.question: In Listing 2.2, what does the argument `512` in `layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")` specify?
options: The number of input pixels of each MNIST image
The number of units (output dimensions) of the layer
The number of training images processed per batch
questions.answer: The number of units (output dimensions) of the layer
questions.explanation: The first positional argument of `Dense` is the number of units, i.e. the size of the representation the layer outputs. The input size (784 pixels) is inferred later; the batch size is set in `fit()` on p.44; and the number of classes (10) is the size of the *second* layer.

questions.question: Why does the last layer have exactly 10 units and a softmax activation?
questions.answer: Because there are 10 digit classes and softmax turns the 10 scores into probabilities that sum to 1, one per class.
questions.explanation: The page calls it a '10-way softmax classification layer' returning 'an array of 10 probability scores (summing to 1)', each the probability that the image belongs to one of the 10 digit classes.

questions.question: Explain the authors' description of a layer as a 'filter' and of a model as a 'sieve'. What is being filtered, and what does 'progressive data distillation' mean?
questions.answer: A layer takes data in and outputs a representation that is more useful for the task; chaining layers refines the representation step by step, so the information relevant to the problem is progressively concentrated (distilled) while irrelevant detail is left behind, like material passing through a succession of finer sieves.
questions.explanation: The page says layers 'extract representations out of the data fed into them—hopefully, representations that are more meaningful for the problem at hand', and that deep learning chains simple layers into 'a form of progressive data distillation'.

questions.question: Which of the three compile ingredients does NOT influence how the weights are updated during training?
options: All three influence the weight updates
questions.explanation: Metrics are 'to monitor during training and testing'; they are reported, not optimized. The loss is what the model uses to 'steer itself in the right direction', and the optimizer is 'the mechanism through which the model will update itself'.

questions.question: Once the input is flattened to 784 values (p.44), how many learnable parameters does the model of Listing 2.2 have? Show the computation.
questions.answer: 784*512 + 512 = 401,920 for the first layer; 512*10 + 10 = 5,130 for the second; total 407,050.
questions.explanation: A Dense layer has a weight matrix of shape (inputs, units) plus one bias per unit, so its parameter count is inputs*units + units. Adding both layers gives 407,050. (The formula comes from the Dense computation `dot(input, W) + b` spelled out on p.76.)

questions.question: What does `optimizer="adam"` in Listing 2.3 do, in the terms used on this page?
questions.answer: It selects the optimizer, i.e. the mechanism through which the model will update itself based on the training data it sees, to improve its performance.
questions.explanation: The page defines the optimizer bullet exactly this way; `"adam"` names one particular optimizer (a variant of stochastic gradient descent, covered from p.63).

questions.question: Without looking, write Listing 2.2 from memory, then list the three things that must be chosen at compilation and one sentence on the role of each.
questions.answer: `model = keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(512, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])`; loss function (measures performance to steer learning), optimizer (updates the weights), metrics (monitored, here accuracy).
